assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED made strong, controllable light-matter coupling available on a chip: a superconducting artificial atom coupled to a microwave resonator, giving dispersive readout, photon-mediated qubit coupling and the architecture used by essentially all superconducting quantum processors. It is original, clearly defined and has had lasting impact on quantum technology and microwave quantum optics.
assessment.attribution: The 2004 theory proposal (Blais with Schoelkopf's and Wallraff's circle) and the first strong-coupling experiments (Wallraff, Schoelkopf and collaborators) give a natural theory-plus-two-experiments trio. Other contributors to the Yale and ETH programmes and to the underlying qubit work (including the macroscopic-quantum-circuit work already recognised in 2025) are not on the list, so the line of credit is somewhat blurred.
assessment.maturity: Strong and independent confirmation by many groups worldwide over two decades; the framework is stable and routinely used. Timing is reasonable, although the 2025 prize was in the neighbouring area of superconducting circuits, so the committee would need to argue that this is a distinct discovery rather than a continuation.
uncertainties: Field proximity to my own research and to the programme I direct means I may overrate this candidate; I treat that as a bias to discount, not evidence.
Whether the committee would see it as sufficiently separate from the 2025 award.
Whether the credit should include other early theorists or experimentalists not on the supplied list.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal for quantum logic with trapped ions and its experimental realisation defined how a programmable quantum computer could be built from well-isolated quantum systems. It had broad influence on quantum information and on high-fidelity gates and entanglement.
assessment.attribution: A theory pair plus a leading experimentalist is a coherent configuration. The 2012 prize to Wineland and Haroche covered manipulation of single quantum systems, which overlaps with this field, and other ion-trap groups (e.g. NIST and Innsbruck colleagues) contributed decisively, so the allocation among experimentalists is genuinely contested.
assessment.maturity: Roughly three decades of confirmation across many laboratories, with commercial platforms built on it. Mature. The main timing question is the extent to which earlier prizes already recognised the experimental foundations.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 prize on ion manipulation.
Which experimental leaders besides Blatt deserve equal credit.
Overlap with B033 and with lattice quantum simulation if Zoller or Cirac are recognised elsewhere.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: BB84, entanglement-based key distribution and quantum teleportation founded quantum cryptography and quantum communication, linking foundations to information security and quantum networks. The conceptual originality and breadth of impact are very high.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard are the clear originators of BB84 and teleportation; Ekert's 1991 protocol is the entanglement-based counterpart. This is a natural three-person configuration. Teleportation also had co-authors (a larger group in 1993) and experimental demonstrators already recognised in 2022, so the text should be framed around the protocols.
assessment.maturity: Decades of experimental implementation and commercial systems; the underlying ideas are stable. Recognition is overdue rather than premature. The 2022 prize for entanglement experiments partly prepared the ground.
uncertainties: Teleportation was a six-author paper, so credit beyond the listed names exists.
Ballots B002 and B027 describe essentially the same credit group; this ballot covers both protocol and teleportation aspects.
Practical security of real QKD devices is still debated, though the theoretical contribution is not.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock combined magic-wavelength trapping with optical transitions to reach stability and accuracy beyond caesium and earlier ion clocks, and it is a platform for tests of fundamental physics and relativistic geodesy. Its importance for precision measurement is large and growing.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice idea; Ye led demonstration of the highest-performance clocks. Other contributors (including optical-clock and frequency-comb work already recognised in 2005 and the ion clock work recognised in 2012) are credited elsewhere. A two-laureate configuration is fair.
assessment.maturity: Independently confirmed in many national laboratories, with a redefinition of the second under discussion. It is mature in performance but the practical redefinition is still pending, which makes timing plausible but not urgent.
uncertainties: Overlap with earlier clock-related prizes.
Whether the redefinition of the second would be needed first for the committee's taste.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Loss-DiVincenzo proposal of spin qubits in quantum dots and the experimental realisation of single-spin control and two-qubit gates opened a path to semiconductor quantum computing compatible with industrial fabrication. It is an important parallel to superconducting circuits.
assessment.attribution: Loss and DiVincenzo for the theory and Vandersypen for the experiment. Other experimental groups (Delft, Tarucha, Petta, Dzurak, Morello) contributed substantially, so the experimental credit is not clean.
assessment.maturity: Rapid progress in fidelity and scale in the last decade, but the platform has not yet shown the scale of superconducting or ion systems; it is strong but arguably still maturing.
uncertainties: Premature relative to the platform's eventual scaling.
Experimental credit is spread across many groups.
I do not have independent knowledge of the latest fidelity benchmarks.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators created a new classification of electronic phases with robust edge and surface states, with large conceptual impact across condensed matter, topological materials and quantum devices.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the original theoretical prediction; Molenkamp's group gave the first experimental realisation in HgTe quantum wells (following the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal). Other theorists (Bernevig, Zhang, Fu, Moore and others) have a legitimate claim, so a three-person selection leaves out important contributors.
assessment.maturity: Thoroughly confirmed by many materials and measurements for over fifteen years. It is mature and arguably overdue, while the 2016 topological prize addressed related but distinct earlier work.
uncertainties: Credit allocation among the many theorists and experimentalists is contested.
Interaction with the 2016 prize on topological phase transitions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ground-state cooling and quantum control of mechanical oscillators, including quantum states of motion and entanglement with light or circuits, extend quantum phenomena to macroscopic objects and give sensors and transducers. It is close to the physics the 2025 prize emphasised, using related circuit and microwave techniques.
assessment.attribution: Cleland made the first quantum ground-state and qubit-coupled mechanical demonstrations, Teufel the sideband cooling of a micromechanical oscillator in a microwave circuit, and Aspelmeyer cavity optomechanics. Other groups (Painter, Lehnert, Kippenberg, Regal) are important, so the line is contestable.
assessment.maturity: Experimentally well confirmed, but the field is still developing and its applications are not yet decisive; reasonably mature but earlier than the other fields I ranked above.
uncertainties: Whether a prize here would be seen as too close to the 2025 award.
Large number of equally deserving groups.
My familiarity with the circuit-based side may bias me.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realised quantum simulation of strongly correlated matter, such as the superfluid to Mott insulator transition and single-site-resolved Hubbard physics. It provides a quantum simulator at a scale and control level beyond classical computation in some regimes.
assessment.attribution: Zoller and collaborators supplied the theory (Jaksch et al.) , Bloch and Greiner the experiments (Greiner et al. 2002 and quantum gas microscopes). Greiner's microscope and the Hänsch/Kasevich/Esslinger groups also deserve credit, and Zoller's overlap with B022 and B033 makes a joint awarding awkward.
assessment.maturity: Widely confirmed and now a mature field; analogue simulators have solved real problems. Timing is right but is not urgent compared with those above.
uncertainties: Overlap in Zoller's credit with trapped-ion theory.
Contributions of other groups to lattice experiments and quantum gas microscopes.
